title: Safety, the National Grid and the Cost of Electricity
summary: Electrical safety devices, how electricity is generated and distributed through the national grid, and calculating the cost of electrical energy in kWh.

notes.text: Mains electricity in South Africa is **230 V AC**, which can kill. Household circuits contain safety devices that cut off the current when something goes wrong.

rows: A thin wire that melts when the current is too high, breaking the circuit
A switch in the distribution board that trips (opens) when the current is too high; it can be reset
Trips when current leaks to earth (for example through a person), preventing electric shock
Connects the metal casing of an appliance to the ground so that a fault current flows safely away
Plastic coating on wires and plugs stops current from reaching people

items: Never overload a plug point with many adaptors.
Do not touch switches or appliances with wet hands; keep appliances away from water.
Illegal connections (*izinyoka*) cause fires, electrocution and power cuts.
Stay away from fallen power lines and substations.

notes.text: Most of South Africa's electricity is produced in **coal-fired power stations** in Mpumalanga and Limpopo. Coal is burned to boil water; the **steam** turns **turbines**, which turn **generators** that convert kinetic energy into electrical energy.

notes.caption: Energy conversions in a coal power station
Other sources of electricity
rows: Uses water pumped up when demand is low
Wind farms in the Eastern and Western Cape
Solar parks in the Northern Cape; rooftop panels

notes.label: Remember
notes.text: Burning coal releases carbon dioxide (a greenhouse gas) and sulfur dioxide (which causes acid rain). Renewable sources produce far less pollution, but wind and solar depend on the weather.

The **national grid** is the network of power lines that carries electricity from power stations to users across the country. **Step-up transformers** raise the voltage to very high values (up to 765 000 V) so that less energy is lost as heat in the long lines. **Step-down transformers** at substations reduce it to 230 V for homes.
Power and the cost of electricity
The rate at which an appliance uses energy, measured in watts (W) or kilowatts (kW). 1 kW = 1 000 W.

notes.caption: Electricity is sold in kilowatt-hours (kWh), sometimes called units

notes.title: Calculating cost
notes.problem: A 2 000 W kettle is used for a total of 30 minutes a day. Electricity costs R2,50 per kWh. Calculate the cost per day.
steps: Power = 2 000 W = 2 kW; time = 30 min = 0,5 h

items: Switch off lights and appliances when not in use.
Install a solar water heater or geyser blanket; set the geyser lower.
Boil only the water you need.

questions.prompt: Give ONE advantage and TWO disadvantages of generating electricity from coal.
questions.memo:
Advantage (1): coal is plentiful/cheap in South Africa; reliable supply day and night
Disadvantages (1 each): produces CO₂ / greenhouse gases; causes acid rain (SO₂); non-renewable; mining damages land; uses lots of water

questions.prompt: Suggest TWO ways a family can reduce its electricity bill.
questions.memo: Any two (1 each): switch off unused appliances; LED bulbs; solar geyser / geyser blanket; boil only needed water; use appliances efficiently
